title: Rapid Fire
subtitle: Keep up - fast calls, real situations, no time to overthink.
whyThisMatters: Attackers count on you deciding in the first three seconds, before you have time to think. Practising the pause now helps it become automatic later.
rememberThis: When something pushes you to act fast, that pressure itself is the warning sign.

discussionPrompts: Ask how it felt to decide under time pressure. Was the pause even harder with a quiz clock running?
For the CFO video call question, ask if anyone would feel okay ending a call with a senior leader to go and check.
Ask the group to name their own trusted way to check an urgent request. Do this for each role shown here: Finance, HR, Operations, and Offshore.
facilitatorNotes.commonWrongAnswer: People most often get q1 wrong. It is the CFO video call. They choose "approve the payment" because the face and voice matched. A live call feels harder to fake than an email.

questions.question: You are on a video call with someone who looks and sounds exactly like your CFO. Their picture freezes for a second and the lighting looks a little off. But they speak with full confidence. They ask you to approve an unusual payment right now, before the call ends. What do you check first?
choices: Approve the payment - the face and voice matched, so it must really be them
Quietly stall by saying you'll do it after the call, hoping they forget
End the call and verify the request by contacting your CFO through a number or channel you already know is real
Ask a coworker in chat if they got the same request, then decide
questions.explanation: A real-looking face and voice on a call is not proof of identity. Both can be faked. An unusual, urgent payment is exactly when to STOP and VERIFY using a channel you already trust. Never use a channel given to you in the same call. Then REPORT anything strange.

questions.question: A message looks like it is from your usual hiring site. It forwards a promising candidate CV as an attachment. But the sender address is spelled a little differently than normal. It says the candidate needs an answer "within the hour" or they will take another offer. What should you do?
choices: Open the attachment quickly so you don't lose a strong candidate
Reply to the sender asking for more information
STOP before opening anything, VERIFY the sender's exact email address and the platform directly, then REPORT if it doesn't check out
Forward it to a colleague and let them decide
questions.explanation: A small spelling change in the sender address plus fake urgency is a classic trap. Attackers know HR often gets attachments from strangers. STOP, VERIFY, and REPORT applies to a "candidate" file just like any other email.

questions.question: You get a Teams message from someone you do not know. No photo, no chat history. They say the site supervisor cannot be reached. They ask you to skip the permit-to-work sign-off on a job "just this once" so the schedule does not slip. What is the warning sign?
choices: It's fine - schedules matter, and you can sort out the paperwork later
Someone with no verified identity is pressuring you to skip a safety check, using urgency and unreachability as the excuse
It's a normal, routine reminder about the schedule
It's expected - supervisors often message from other accounts
questions.explanation: An unknown sender, time pressure, and a request to skip a safety check are the warning signs. Skipping a check because an urgent, unreachable person said so is the red flag. It is the same pattern as a fake CEO asking for a wire transfer. Here it targets a safety step instead of money.

questions.question: You get a text about your crew change schedule and tap the link without looking closely. A second later, the page that opened looks strange. What is the correct first step?
choices: Ignore it and hope nothing happens
Report it right away through the proper channel - don't try to fix it yourself first
Delete the text so no one finds out
Wait until you're back onshore to mention it
questions.explanation: Fast reporting, not silence or trying to fix it yourself, gives IT the best chance to limit damage. This is true on shore or offshore with limited internet.

questions.question: An email feels a little strange, but you are not sure if it is harmful. Why does reporting it anyway still matter?
choices: Security teams would rather check a false alarm than miss a real one
Only IT is responsible for noticing anything unusual
Flagging things you're unsure about wastes everyone's time
It's better to just ask a coworker first instead of the official channel
questions.explanation: Not reporting is far more costly than reporting too much. Every report, sure or not, is a chance to catch something early. This is true for every team.

stopVerifyReportPrompts.scenario: A person you do not know with no visible badge asks you to hold the server room door open for them. They say their badge "is not scanning."
stopVerifyReportPrompts.idealResponse: STOP - do not hold the door. VERIFY their access with reception or security. REPORT the attempt.

stopVerifyReportPrompts.scenario: A "vendor" emails asking you to change the bank account for an upcoming payment. They say it is a routine update.
stopVerifyReportPrompts.idealResponse: STOP - do not change payment details from an email alone. VERIFY by phone using a number you already have on file. REPORT the request.

stopVerifyReportPrompts.scenario: A coworker gets a text "from HR" asking them to click a link and update payroll details right away.
stopVerifyReportPrompts.idealResponse: STOP - do not click. VERIFY using the official HR portal or a known contact. REPORT it to IT or security.

stopVerifyReportPrompts.scenario: While using a shared laptop, a pop-up says the computer has a virus. It tells you to call a number on the screen right now to fix it.
stopVerifyReportPrompts.idealResponse: STOP - do not call the number. VERIFY with your real IT helpdesk using a known number. REPORT the pop-up.

stopVerifyReportPrompts.scenario: A voicemail sounds exactly like your CEO. It asks for an urgent favor with gift cards, right before an important meeting.
stopVerifyReportPrompts.idealResponse: STOP - do not buy anything. VERIFY directly with the CEO through a separate, trusted channel. REPORT the voicemail.
